characters: Adoley: an energetic nine-year-old Ghanaian girl with neat cornrows, wearing a bright red-and-gold school PE T-shirt, navy athletic shorts, and white trainers.
Mr Kotei: her warm, athletic Ghanaian PE teacher wearing a royal-blue tracksuit with white stripes, trainers, and a silver whistle on a neck cord.

narrationPlan.voice: A lively girl’s voice for Adoley; a warm, clear PE teacher’s voice for Mr Kotei
narrationPlan.pace: Brisk during the run, calm in the explanations (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A steady drum that speeds up during the run and slows down at rest (placeholder)
culturalNotes: PE lessons, ampe, skipping, and football are part of everyday school life across Ghana.
World Health Organization guidelines recommend an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity for children and adolescents aged 5–17.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Confirm the grade-level clarity of how lungs, blood, heart, and muscles work together during exercise.
Confirm the 60-minute daily physical activity recommendation with Ghana Health Service / WHO guidance.

teacherGuide.overview: An active science story connecting Physical Education with how the heart, lungs, and muscles work together, paired with hydration and safety awareness.
learningGoals: Explain why breathing and heart rate speed up during exercise.
Name the roles of the lungs, heart, and muscles.
State two safety habits for active play (drinking water and stopping if dizzy or in pain).
beforeReading: Have learners sit quietly, place a hand on their chest or wrist, and notice their resting beat.
whileReading: Pause on page 3 so pairs can retell the air-to-lungs-to-heart-to-muscles link in their own words.
afterReading: March or jog gently on the spot for 30–60 seconds (for learners who are well) and compare resting vs. active heartbeats.
List three favourite active games that keep our hearts strong.
discussion: Why did Adoley’s heartbeat slow down again in the shade?
Why is drinking clean water important when we play in warm weather?
reflection: Which active game will you play for movement today?

mathsExtension.task: Suppose a resting pulse is 20 beats in 15 seconds. Multiply by 4 to find beats in 1 minute.
Suppose a pulse is 80 beats per minute at rest and 120 after running. How many more beats per minute is that?

support: Tap a slow desk beat for rest and a quicker beat for running so learners can hear the difference.
stretch: Write three sentences explaining how oxygen reaches leg muscles during a football match.

culturalNotes: PE lessons, ampe, skipping, and football are part of everyday school life across Ghana.
World Health Organization guidelines recommend an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity for children and adolescents aged 5–17.
localiseThis: Include local games such as ampe, pilolo, skipping, and football.
Excuse any unwell learner from vigorous movement and remind all pupils to report dizziness immediately.

factCheck.claim: School-age children need about 60 minutes of active physical play each day, and heart and breathing rates rise during exercise to deliver oxygen to working muscles.
factCheck.explanation: Active muscles consume oxygen faster, prompting faster breathing and cardiac output; daily moderate-to-vigorous movement strengthens cardiovascular health.
factCheck.reference: World Health Organization (2020) Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour (ages 5–17)
